name: Planning Fallacy
description: People often predict that tasks or projects will finish sooner than they actually do, especially when they focus on the ideal plan instead of comparable past outcomes. The broad 'people always underestimate time' version is more overstated than the evidence supports.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to product scoping, delivery commitments, research planning, migration estimates, and roadmap promises where teams model the happy path and discount precedent.
prevalence_note: Widely referenced in product, delivery, and behavioral-design discussions about estimation and roadmap optimism, though less central in pure interaction-design curricula than classic UI laws.

findings.description: An integrative review across psychology, engineering, and management-science literatures found underestimation of task/project time was consistently reported in engineering and management studies, but NOT consistently found in studies from the psychology literature — the popularized 'people always underestimate how long things take' framing oversimplifies a more mixed, context-dependent evidence base. The review also directly challenges the common claim that small tasks get overestimated and large tasks underestimated, suggesting this may partly be a statistical artifact of random error rather than a real psychological effect.
findings.source_title: From Origami to Software Development: A Review of Studies on Judgment-Based Predictions of Performance Time

findings.description: Predictions of task completion times were consistently too optimistic across academic and nonacademic tasks. People focused on future plan-based scenarios rather than relevant past experience when predicting — but when explicitly prompted to connect their predictions to past experience, the optimistic bias was eliminated. Predicting for OTHER people showed the opposite pattern: observers overestimated completion times and drew more on past experience. Per secondary characterization: 37 psychology students predicting their thesis completion time estimated a worst-case average of 48.6 days, but actual average completion took 55.5 days — worse than their own worst case — and only about 30% finished on their predicted schedule.
findings.effect_size: worst-case estimate ~48.6 days vs. actual completion ~55.5 days; only ~30% finished on predicted schedule (per secondary characterization, not stated numerically in the abstract itself)
findings.source_title: Exploring the "Planning Fallacy": Why People Underestimate Their Task Completion Times
findings.source_venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

applications.title: The 2017 US tax bill debate and the planning fallacy in retirement savings
applications.description: During the 2017 US congressional tax bill debate, commentary on proposed changes to 401(k) contribution limits drew on the planning fallacy to explain why lowering pretax savings caps could suppress retirement savings overall: people who delay saving, expecting to make up the gap later, generally do not follow through. At the time, according to the US Government Accountability Office, only about half of US households aged 55 and older used any retirement savings vehicle (a 401(k) or an IRA) at all.
applications.ethical_note: This is a policy-analysis case about a real legislative debate and a real government statistic, not a persuasion or product-design scenario -- there is no party attempting to influence user behavior through UI design here, only a commentary connecting a cognitive bias to a real policy stake.
